World.title: Photographer accused of stealing Bondi terror attack victim's camera
World.content:
A photographer who allegedly stole a Bondi terror attack victim's camera, before pawning off the equipment days later, has been charged.

Fifteen people died in the shooting at Bondi Beach on December 14, 2025, with gunman Naveed Akram later charged with murder and terrorism offences.

Officers investigating the attack identified that one of the victims, retired police officer and photographer Peter Meagher, had his camera equipment stolen after the attack.

Peter Meagher, a former NSW Police officer, was killed in the Bondi terror attack. (Supplied)

Police yesterday seized a camera, handcuffs and electronic devices during a search in Marayong in Sydney's west.

A 35-year-old man was arrested and taken to Riverstone Police Station, where he was charged with stealing offences, weapons and drug offences.

Police will allege the man was a photographer at the Hanukkah event targeted in the shooting who stole Mr Meagher's camera equipment before pawning it days later.

He was granted bail and is due to front Blacktown Local Court next month.

World.title: Pendlebury's 433rd game simply his latest of many AFL records
World.content:
The names of 14 players span the history of the AFL, from its breakaway from the VFA in 1897 to the spectacle we know today.

Charlie Panham to Fred Elliott to Jock McHale to Vic Thorp to Gordon Coventry to Jack Dyer to Dick Reynolds to Ted Whitten to John Nicholls to Kevin Murray to John Rantall to Kevin Bartlett to Michael Tuck to Scott Pendlebury.

The chain above goes some way to explaining how football has evolved. The list contains pioneers and groundbreakers, innovators and some of the finest to ever step onto a football field. While the football of a century ago may only be vaguely reminiscent of its modern counterpart, those fourteen names create a clear link from then to now.

This week the last of these names is firmly in the spotlight. Scott Pendlebury is on the cusp of claiming the AFL games record — the one key item those fourteen names have in common. It's yet another title and record added to Pendlebury's overstuffed pool room. When Pendlebury dons his gold-tinged guernsey against West Coast on Saturday he will start adding to his lead.

The games record joins other marks such as most disposals, most handballs and most goal assists. These intangible accolades jostle for space alongside his two premierships, six All-Australian blazers, five Copeland Trophies and three Bob Rose–Charlie Sutton Medals, amongst other awards.

Pendlebury's honours board only scratches the surface of who is as a footballer, however. What makes him so special, and will anyone chase his records down?

Pendlebury's brilliance

Pendlebury's ability to find time and space has been one of the most redeeming qualifies of his game. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Given the length of his career, Pendlebury has been talked about more than most players.

Chapter and verse have been penned about his ability to create time and space with the ball, and his class on the field. Pendlebury standing still while the world rushes around him has entered the footballing lexicon like Buddy's arc.

As has his "basketball background", despite not being the only player to play another sport during his youth.

What is less discussed is what drove both entries into footballing lore — namely his work rate and dedication. In 2019 former teammate Dane Swan described that intense focus to SEN.

"Obviously he's worked extremely hard, harder than anyone during my time at the club. And it's no surprise that he's achieved what he has," he said.

"It started from day one. His passion, work ethic and training intensity have only improved as he's gone on."

Few players, if any, dedicate themselves to their craft as much as Collingwood's talisman. Stories from Pendlebury's past and present show glimpses of that intense focus. As a budding basketballer he had keys to the gym in Sale in order to hone his game. These days it takes the form of nutritional dedication and ice baths, alongside intense recovery sessions. As a result Pendlebury has barely missed time due to soft tissue injuries.

This dedication follows through to his approach on-field. While Pendlebury has played with an almost countless number of teammates, there is one element that they all share — he made their games better.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"Scott made me a much better player than what I was," Swan explained to SEN.

Since his breakout 2010, when he finished fourth in the Brownlow Medal and the Pies won a premiership, Collingwood have won 62 per cent of games with Scott Pendlebury, which has dropped to 52 per cent in the relatively rare times he's been absent.

While Pendlebury is resolute with ball in hand, much of his excellence happens without the ball. Good players are often said to dominate where the ball is now, while great players anticipate where it will be next. Pendlebury's understanding of the game often means that he finds himself in the right spot before anyone else knows where that will be. That creates the ability to influence games without necessarily dominating the ball — a skill only the best in the sport have.

Since 2012, no player has had more defensive half pressure acts than Pendlebury, despite his reputation as primarily an outside player. Like an iceberg, much of his importance is held in the parts that people can't (or don't readily) see.

But the bits we do regularly see are exceptional. Pendlebury has the record for most career disposals, handballs, tackles, uncontested possessions and goal assists. He also sits within the top 10 of several other categories, including some of the more modern advanced statistics.

In short, Pendlebury's 432 games to date haven't been spent filling a guernsey; he's actively contributed to several extremely successful sides.

Catching greatness

Scott Pendlebury pictured with the fellow legends who have played over 400 VFL/AFL games. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

Every time a record is broken or a mountain summitted, the natural tendency is to think of who will be next.

The most obvious starting spot is looking at who is in the league right now. After all, every games record holder shared a field with his predecessor, with the exception of Tuck and Harvey.

However, the numbers show that this trend may be harder to continue than in previous years. Currently, no player is truly on Pendlebury's record-setting pace. A large part of this is down to the fact that Pendlebury was one of the last players drafted the year they turned 17. This early start meant that the former captain debuted and played nine games in his 18th year — all in the "famous" number 16 guernsey.

As such, Pendlebury had played 32 games by the end of what is now every draftee's first year in the AFL. Even playing every regular season game will leave a new player half a season behind his benchmark.

But some hope remains for the chasing pack. An impending 24-game home and away season provides more margin for error for future players. It's a similar edge that enjoyed Pendlebury over players from earlier eras. In addition, the new finals format means more finals for more teams.

V/AFL seasons have ranged in length from 14 games to the current day 23, with the number of finals also swelling in that time. All in all, the season is up to a third longer than it was at times in the past, which is a big factor in the dramatic increase to the membership ranks of the 400-game club.

Pendlebury's record is also driven by a broader trend across global sport. Careers of elite athletes have generally stretched longer over time, with many record-holders active this decade. While the exact cause is hard to pin down, it is likely that increased pay, advances in sports science and a bigger crop of talent to draw from are behind the surge of recent record setters.

The pack chasing Pendlebury's mark can be broken down into a few groups — elite veterans, id-career marauders and young stars.

A slew of modern-day greats sit roughly a full season behind his pace, headed by Patrick Dangerfield, Lachie Neale and Marcus Bontempelli. This group has a chance to catch Pendlebury's likely end of year games total by their age-40 year, or possibly even a year earlier with a good run of finals appearances. Teammate Steele Sidebottom is also firmly in this category.

However, those most equipped to overtake Pendlebury may be those with a little more time up their sleeves.

The most likely candidate overall is Brisbane's midfielder Hugh McCluggage. The Allansford product is 28 years old and already has 20 finals under his belt after a successful decade at the Lions. McCluggage has played an incredible average of 23.2 games a year for the last nine seasons. Across his career, McCluggage has only missed 10 Lions games, including three earlier this year. Brisbane teammate Harris Andrews also stands a chance, given his durability and regular finals appearances.

There's also a younger group of players like Nick Daicos, Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera, Noah Anderson and Caleb Serong, who are keeping pace early in their careers. Their age means that there is the least room for error in this crop, but they are also able to make best use of the expanded seasons and sports science of modern footy.

Brisbane star Hugh McCluggage is as good a bet as any to challenge Pendlebury's games record. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Five players — Daicos, McCluggage, Connor Macdonald, Nick Blakey and Noah Anderson — are potentially in the frame to even meet Pendlebury's expected total at the end of this season a year younger than Pendlebury is now.

That's if everything breaks just right — from injuries to form and regular finals campaigns. It's a pretty big assumption considering how many players' careers have been derailed for one of those reasons or another. There's a reason that so few players have played 20 years or more of league football — it's very hard to do.

These calculations also only hold if Pendlebury retires at the end of the year — a big if considering his current form and comments in recent days.

"'Fly' [Craig McRae] has said: 'Don't put limits or bring birth certificates into the equation,'" Pendlebury told the media this week.

Pendlebury is still a vital part of Collingwood coach Craig McRae's line-up, even at his advanced age. (AFL Photos via Getty Images: Dylan Burns)

"So I think there is no reason why I can't play on into next season if my form holds."

If Pendlebury decides to run around one year (or maybe more), more records potentially enter his reach. He's currently 32 games behind Craig Bradley's all competitions elite games record, with the South Australian playing 464 games across the SANFL and V/AFL before the Victorian competition became national. One more season might just see Pendlebury break that record.

Pendlebury also sits 41 wins behind Michael Tuck for the most wins played in a career. That mark is unlikely to fall unless he challenges Vic Cumberland's record for oldest player in a game. That mark is perhaps more unlikely, considering Cumberland was 43 when he suited up in 10 games for the Saints in 1920.

The other records

Pendlebury's tackles record could eventually be broken by last year's Brownlow medallist Matt Rowell. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The other five records that Pendlebury holds are in more danger of being overhauled — largely due to changes in the way that the game is being played.

While most of these records only go back to 1999, the game's evolution in that quarter century indicates that they may fall sooner rather than later. Unlike the games record, at least two players are on pace to overhaul each of Pendlebury's major statistical records.

Matt Rowell is the most likely to strike first as he is well on track to breaking the league's tackle record by age 30 — if he can stay fit. By contrast, Pendlebury's disposal mark may be the last one to fall, with only two relatively young players — Nick Daicos and Harry Sheezel — on track currently.

Rowell's assault on the tackles record is emblematic of the changes in football. In the year 2000, teams averaged 31.9 tackles per game. Last year, that number had almost doubled to 60.2. Football is entering a handball and disposal-heavy era, with the number of uncontested possessions rising against contested ball.

As a result, it won't be a surprise if the last record to fall is Pendlebury's impending games record.

When it does, it will spark memories of how great and influential the Pie was on the field — as similar memories flood in about Tuck, Harvey, Bartlett and co this week. Records exist to be broken, and few are more deserving of this one than Pendlebury.

World.title: Snowtown killer James Vlassakis's image has been revealed — here's why
World.content:
James Vlassakis was the youngest of four perpetrators convicted for his role in the notorious "bodies-in-the-barrels" serial killings, which rocked Australia at the turn of the century.

In May 1999, police made the chilling discovery of human remains hidden in barrels secreted in an old bank vault in Snowtown, in South Australia's Mid North.

While Vlassakis's name has always been in the public domain, his image had remained hidden for 25 years due to a suppression on his identity.

A court sketch of Snowtown killer James Vlassakis. (Supplied)

But, on Tuesday, South Australia's highest court lifted a long-running suppression order banning the publication of his image or description of his appearance.

So why has his face been kept secret for so long and why can we identify him now?

Who is James Vlassakis?

James Spyridon Vlassakis was born in December 1979 and was just 18 in mid-1998, when he took part in the murder of his half-brother Troy Youde — a crime he committed at the behest of his stepfather and Snowtown ringleader John Bunting.

It was one of 12 deaths between 1992 and 1999, of which Bunting was convicted of 11 and the other main offender — Robert Wagner — was convicted of 10.

John Bunting and Robert Wagner are serving life sentences without the possibility of parole. (ABC News)

A fourth man Mark Ray Haydon, was involved as an accomplice and convicted of seven counts of assisting an offender, for storing bodies at his home north of Adelaide and for helping to move them.

Vlassakis pleaded guilty to four of the murders.

He was still 18 when he took part in the murders of Fred Brooks in September 1998 and Gary O'Dwyer later that year.

He was also convicted of the May 1999 murder of the last of the victims, David Johnson.

The remains of each of those victims were found at Snowtown.

The old bank at Snowtown where eight bodies were found in barrels in 1999. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Vlassakis was sentenced to life in prison in 2002, with a non-parole period of 26 years.

The sentence was backdated to when he was taken into custody in June 1999.

Because he helped to convict his three co-offenders by giving evidence against them, his image was suppressed for his protection.

How did he become involved?

In 1994, Vlassakis's mother began a relationship with John Bunting, and at times Vlassakis lived with them.

When Vlassakis was sentenced in 2002, Justice Kevin Duggan said he was "besotted" by Bunting, who had "became somewhat of a hero" and father figure to Vlassakis.

Last year, Parole Board chair Frances Nelson KC, said Vlassakis was "drawn to Bunting's behaviour".

Frances Nelson KC said Vlassakis was "terrified of Bunting". (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

"He was terrified of Bunting and Bunting took the place of the man of the house when he was 14 years of age and vulnerable," she said.

Most of the victims were either family or friends of the four men involved.

Why was his identity kept hidden?

Vlassakis was the key witness in the prosecution case against killers John Bunting and Robert Wagner, who are each serving life sentences without the possibility for parole.

James Vlassakis in custody around the late 1990s or early 2000s. (Supplied)

At the time he was sentenced in 2002, Justice Duggan said Vlassakis was not the instigator of any of the murders and had become involved "through someone who had considerable influence over you".

He also noted that, in June 2001, when Vlassakis entered his guilty pleas it "came with an undertaking to assist the police and give evidence against the others who had been charged".

"If it had not been for your plea of guilty, your extensive cooperation with the police and your undertaking to give evidence for the prosecution in the forthcoming trial, I would have imposed a non-parole period of 42 years," Justice Kevin Duggan said.

"I am satisfied that you have given extensive assistance to the police in this matter and I take into account your undertaking to give evidence."

Police officers carry evidence bags out of the old Snowtown bank building early in the investigation into the serial killings. (ABC News)

He said Vlassakis at the time was to be "subjected to close confinement" because he was yet to give evidence at the subsequent trials for Bunting and Wagner.

"Your confinement is likely to be much more restrictive than would otherwise be the case."

Vlassakis's image was also suppressed to protect his identity ahead of giving evidence.

Why can we identify him now?

Last year, the Parole Board granted Vlassakis release on parole, and Ms Nelson explained at the time that he met the legislative criteria and was "genuinely remorseful".

She said his behaviour in custody was "excellent".

"We have to look at whether or not he presents a risk to the community and in our assessment he does not," she said.

A composite image showing a file photo of Snowtown killer James Vlassakis in custody and a court sketch of him 25 years later. (Supplied)

But, he has remained in custody because South Australia's Attorney-General Kyam Maher requested a review of the decision on the grounds that the Parole Board had "erred in granting the prisoner's release".

Parole Administrative Review Commissioner Michael David KC later blocked Vlassakis's release on parole, but the Parole Board lodged proceedings in the SA Supreme Court to review that decision.

The matter came before the court this week, where lawyers for the ABC argued Vlassakis's protection was no longer a valid reason to shield him from the public.

The court accepted those arguments, and revoked the 25-year-old order prohibiting the publication of his image.

That outcome was welcomed by some loved ones of the victims, the state's Commissioner for Victims' Rights said after the suppression lifted.

Sarah Quick says restricting James Vlassakis's image may cause "uncertainty and fear for victims". (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"They've stated that whilst it may be confronting to see his image after all these years, that ultimately it will make them feel safer," Sarah Quick said.

"It's safety in just removing the uncertainty of not knowing what he looks like."

Ms Quick said that, had Vlassakis's image remained suppressed, there would have been "uncertainty and fear for victims, not knowing that they might be in proximity to the offender".

World.title: A year on, survivors still counting cost of '1-in-500-year' disaster
World.content:
Ed Trotter was away when the worst flood on record inundated his home in northern New South Wales, and he was unable to take action as paddocks transformed into lakes.

When he returned to his Glenthorne property, just north of Taree, he was shocked by the devastation.

"It was far worse than what I thought it would be like," he said.

"The way mud just seems to seep through closed doors and get into everything … I basically had to turf almost everything in the house out — bedding, flooring, curtains."

Ed Trotter was away when his house in Glenthorne was inundated in May 2025. (Supplied: Ed Trotter)

That was last May when a "one-in-500-year" flood devastated residents, farmers and businesses across the NSW Mid North Coast.

Mr Trotter spent six months living with friends before he was able to move back to his home.

"The local community and moral support, people with equipment and backhoes and things like that, the local council just clearing … and the road was just under that much mud," he said.

Ed Trotter says after the flood a thick layer of mud covered roads and properties at Glenthorne. (Supplied: Ed Trotter)

Ed Trotter says he had to throw out many possessions in his house. (Supplied: Ed Trotter)

Mr Trotter's property was originally owned by his parents, who ran it as a dairy farm.

He has decided to stay, hoping to "never see a flood like that again in my lifetime" and has taken simple flood-protection measures such as installing more water-resistant flooring.

"This house was actually built by my parents after the big '78 flood, which was as close to a record as any," Mr Trotter said.

"So it was built on silt from that flood, well above the flood level in 2021.

" You could be here for another 100 to 200 years and not see anything like it again, or it could happen next year … it's just one of those things. "

Ed Trotter outside his Glenthorne home on May 29, 2025, about a week after the flood event. (ABC News: Floss Adams)

Residents yet to return home

Across the Mid North Coast, many other flood survivors are still finding their feet, with some yet to move back into their homes.

For those residents, the focus remains on making properties habitable, with flood proofing often limited to using more water-resistant materials in rebuilds.

Wingham was one of the worst-hit areas, and the local Manning Valley Neighbourhood Service, funded by the NSW Reconstruction Authority, has so far supported more than 600 people.

A year after the natural disaster, it is still taking on new cases.

"In February and March alone we had 14 new intakes," centre manager Kate Darnell said.

Kate Darnell says they have helped 600 people and some people are accessing support now for the first time. (ABC News: Emma Siossian)

" We have people to this day that are still couch surfing, are still technically homeless; still bathrooms and kitchens that are not habitable. "

Wingham resident and SES volunteer Bruce Sanders said he initially felt reluctant to seek help, considering others to be in greater need, and spent months using a caravan bathroom.

Bruce Sanders still lives with no kitchen or bathroom 12 months on from the Wingham floods. (ABC News: Emma Siossian)

"My house has still got no kitchen and no bathroom, but I've now got an ensuite that works so we don't have to go outside to go to the loo anymore," he said.

Farmers stay and rebuild

Just north of Taree on the Manning River, Croki on Jones Island was hit hard.

Fifth-generation dairy farmer Craig Emerton and his wife Debbie were forced to swim to an oyster barge with their dog to be evacuated.

Craig Emerton estimates their losses are about half a million dollars. (ABC News: Emma Siossian)

They lost 80 cows and it was four months before they could move back into their home.

"It's been tough," Mr Emerton said.

" Our total losses, probably estimate half a million dollars; we're only a very small dairy. "

Debbie Emerton sits at a table in her flooded home in May 2025. (Supplied: Craig Emerton)

Loading...

Mr Emerton said he was slowly building back his herd, but was still about 25 per cent down on milk production.

"The rain stopped at the end of August and hasn't started properly again … we're basically in drought. We've got a green drought," he said.

" We've been flat out sowing our winter feed. Now with fuel prices, fertiliser prices, it's just making it harder and harder. "

Craig Emerton has built a larger cattle mound in preparation for the next flood. (ABC News: Emma Siossian)

The Emertons have weathered a number of floods over the years, but have decided to stay.

"We love the area. We couldn't sell at the moment if we wanted to. There are places for sale, but nothing is selling on the flood plain," Mr Emerton said.

"I've lived in this house all my life. My great-great-grandfather bought the original farm in 1856."

Mr Emerton has created an additional raised flood mound for his cattle, above the 2025 flood level, and they have made some adjustments to their home, including higher storage areas.

The Emertons say community support has kept them positive. (ABC News: Emma Siossian)

"It's starting to feel a bit like home. We've been very cared for, and we can feel it," Ms Emerton said.

The cost of catastrophe

The swollen Manning River threatened to overtop the Martin Bridge in Taree in May 2025. (Supplied: Stan Groves)

In April, an extra $56.3 million in federal-state disaster recovery funding was announced, including an extra $25,000 grant for directly impacted small businesses and non-profit organisations.

The MidCoast Council said the total flood recovery cost was estimated to be about $281 million.

It has spent $49 million so far, with some key public infrastructure, including bridges that link communities, yet to be replaced.

The Bight Bridge, which connects Tinonee and Wingham, is yet to be repaired. (ABC News: Emma Siossian)

The council's director of infrastructure and engineering services, Robert Scott, said flood mitigation work was primarily being done at a grassroots level by residents using recommended materials in rebuilds.

"It was an extreme flood event, a one-in-500-year flood event, and it means trying to predict and protect properties in such an event is very costly," he said.

"So it's very difficult for broadscale measures to be implemented.

"I think what the last year has taught us, is by being more prepared, by being more resilient in our approach as individuals...having a clear view of when you're going to leave...we are able to mitigate the impact of the floods."

World.title: Man charged with kidnapping Marvin Oraiha months before his alleged murder
World.content:
A man has been charged over the alleged kidnapping of a low-level bikie associate who was shot dead in Sydney's west three years ago.

Marvin Oraiha, 24, was shot in his car in Elizabeth Hills on May 22, 2023, and died at the scene.

It is believed he was loosely linked to the Comanchero bikie gang but police at the time said they were not previously aware of him.

Investigations under Strike Force Hackenburg identified that before Mr Oraiha was fatally shot he was kidnapped by an organised criminal network months earlier in March 2023.

Family sent images of injuries

Police will allege Mr Oraiha was detained overnight at a unit in Belfield and demands for payment of a ransom were made.

Police said his family was sent images of Mr Oraiha with significant head injuries.

Marvin Oraiha, aged in his 20s, was shot while sitting in a car on a Western Sydney street. (Facebook)

Detectives on Wednesday morning arrested a 27-year-old in Dawes Point, locating $31,700 in cash during a search of the man's car.

He was taken to Day Street Police Station and charged with with take/detain in company with intent to ransom occasion actual bodily harm, and participate in a criminal group contributing to criminal activity.

The man was refused bail to appear in court on Thursday.

Two months after Mr Oraiha's death police charged Simione Lua, 22, with murder.

Police at the time said they believed multiple people were involved in Mr Oraiha's alleged murder.

World.title: Recycling scheme contractor accused of having employees sleep on depot floor sues for $5m
World.content:
Allegations that a depot operator in Queensland's container exchange recycling program conducted itself in a manner that could be likened to modern slavery have been detailed during a court hearing in a multi-million dollar federal court dispute.

The claims were made in response to a lawsuit depot operator U Can Recycle filed against Container Exchange (COEX), which the Queensland government appointed to manage the Containers for Change scheme, that claimed COEX had acted unconscionably in threatening to end the parties' contract.

U Can Recycle further alleged, in a separate, related lawsuit, it was misled into believing it would be the operator of a new depot, in which it asked for $5 million in damages.

U Can Recycle is contracted by COEX to run cash refund points across Brisbane and Wide Bay.

It comes as COEX has had 10 allegations referred to the Crime and Corruption Commission (CCC) following an inquiry by the Health, Environment and Innovation Committee last year. The CCC said it does not confirm or comment on any complaints or investigations.

Depot dispute

The first claim by U Can Recycle relates to a new depot in the Logan suburb of Beenleigh, south of Brisbane.

U Can Recycle alleged in court documents that in December 2024, a COEX employee told the business it was the preferred operator for the new depot.

The business alleged the COEX employee told it to begin "mobilisation" — the process of preparing a lease, training, and buying equipment before a cash refund point can operate — "at their earliest convenience".

U Can Recycle operates multiple cash refund points in Queensland. (Supplied)

U Can Recycle said it signed a lease, obtained a traffic management plan, purchased forklifts, reverse vending machines and other equipment and said it provided supporting documents to COEX.

COEX denied it told the operator to begin the mobilisation process; instead, COEX said it told U Can Recycle to prepare a plan that could be carried out in the following year, should the parties' existing contract be varied to include the new depot.

U Can Recycle has argued COEX had misled it into believing it would be the operator for the Beenleigh depot and asked for $5,000,760 in damages for lease loss, mobilisation costs and lost profits over five years.

Concerns raised

According to court documents, in March 2025, COEX raised numerous concerns about the operation of U Can Recycle's depots.

In its defence, COEX alleged U Can Recycle employees were sleeping on mattresses on the floor of a refund point, employees were paying refunds without completing counting, dogs roamed freely with faeces and urine evident, and staff were working outside of their visa requirements.

During a strike-out hearing in the Federal Court in Queensland on Wednesday, barrister Richard Perry, acting for COEX, showed photographs of mattresses on the floors of small rooms, which he said employees on student visas were living in, likening the conditions to conduct that may amount to modern slavery.

"It is asserted by COEX these people are at real risk of exploitation," he said.

In a statement to the ABC a U Can Recycle spokesman said the claims made by COEX were "exaggerated and unfair."

"These include COEX raiding four sites operated by U Can Recycle on the same day and time in the aftermath of Cyclone Alfred, claiming the sites were 'disorderly'," he said.

"COEX banned U Can Recycle from keeping a guard dog at a premises after hours for security purposes. U Can Recycle disputes accusations including that staff were not properly paid and that managers were not present.

"On some occasions, U Can Recycle has agreed to recommendations from COEX but has questioned the manner in which COEX has addressed those matters."

According to court documents, in a letter dated July 22, 2025, COEX indicated U Can Recycle would not be the operator of the Beenleigh facility.

On the same date, COEX sent U Can Recycle a show cause notice, which set out eight allegations of "conduct of behaviour of concern".

COEX alleged the conduct showed the operator was not a "fit and proper person."

'Aggressive' visits

U Can Recycle said since issuing the notice, COEX had visited its depots on numerous occasions, and the visits were "aggressive in nature" and generally had no advanced warning.

The operator alleged during the visits COEX searched the personal possessions of staff, private vehicles and questioned staff on their religious practices.

It further alleged COEX had not acted in good faith or fairly and had not given U Can Recycle a fair opportunity to remedy any of the alleged breaches in the show cause notice.

U Can Recycle alleged COEX had visited depots on numerous occasions generally without warning. (Supplied)

The claims that COEX had acted unconscionably were the subject of Wednesday's strike-out hearing.

Mr Perry disputed the allegations that COEX had continued to threaten to terminate the parties' contract, as no action had been taken since the show cause notice was issued.

U Can Recycle's barrister Douglas Campbell said while the individual matters may not be considered unconscionable on their own, the collective alleged conduct by COEX was.

The court heard the decision on U Can Reycle's contract had been delegated out by the COEX board and no decision on if it should be terminated had been made to date.

A decision on the strike-out hearing is yet to be made.

U Can Recycle further argued that none of the conduct outlined in the show cause notice could reasonably determine that the operator was not a fit and proper person.

It is asking the court to declare that the show cause notice is withdrawn or voided, a clause in the contract should be voided and for damages for loss suffered as a result of the show cause notice, reputational harm and loss of business opportunities.

A COEX spokesperson said it does not comment on matters before the court.

World.title: Advocates critique government's delay on price caps for at-home aged care services
World.content:
In the latest example the rollout of the new aged care system is not going to plan, the government has indefinitely delayed setting price caps for services provided through the Support at Home program, like cleaning, transport and physical therapy.

Price caps were due to be introduced in July this year to ensure recipients were not overcharged, as providers change their costings in line with the new fee structure that began in November.

Instead, the government is in the meantime giving the Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission the go ahead to "order" refunds from providers who overcharge.

Refunds but no price caps for older Australians Support at Home program price caps, due to start in July, have been deferred indefinitely.

But aged care and disability advocate, Peter Willcocks, said it was not an effective solution.

"I think it's a total joke," he said.

Mr Willcocks believed providers would "come up with a spin" to justify their charges, leaving participants vulnerable to high prices.

"We aren't talking about minor amounts," he said, referring to his own experience of being charged a "disgusting" $240 for a lymphatic massage.

But the government insisted regulatory action would not purely rely on complaints from affected people, rather the department and regulator would also both monitor prices.

Minister points to 'global volatility' as reason for delay

Aged Care Minister Sam Rae previously said price caps would "ensure that no older person is inappropriately charged for the services".

But this week he argued the government needed more time, warning "global volatility" risked not getting the price settings right to both protect participants and keep the sector viable.

Health Minister Mark Butler also used the National Disability Insurance Scheme as an example of where, when price caps are set too high, providers all increase their fees to charge the maximum, rather than using it as a ceiling.

Mark Butler. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The Older Persons Advocacy Network's Samantha Edmonds said while she understood the government's reason for the delay, she was concerned it did not give participants the certainty to plan ahead, nor was there any guarantee price volatility would improve.

Although she did back-in the refund mechanism as part of a new "suite of protections" which included publishing quarterly data on median fees and encouraging providers to limit price increases to twice a year.

Older people risk losing some at-home services Price hikes for older people accessing support at home could mean their aged care packages will not stretch as far.

But Centre Alliance MP Rebekha Sharkie said the price cap delay amounted to a broken promise and warned many older people would find the refunds process cumbersome.

"To put the burden on the participant rather than the government having fees capped for providers is fundamentally unfair, I think a lot of people won't even have capacity to do this," she said.

Ms Sharkie also pointed out it would require participants to pay the higher costs in the first place, which could leave people "compromised financially".

Department and regulator to investigate overcharging

Mr Rae said so far the regulator had not found evidence of "systemic price rorting" but there was "inappropriate pricing behaviour [in] some small elements of the sector who are doing the wrong thing".

"So, the package that we've announced is all about cracking down hard on that inappropriate pricing [and] making sure that we've got the best possible protections in place for older people to get the care they need without getting ripped off along the way," he told a Cairns radio station.

He said the range of new measures gave people "the full backing of the Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission in combating unfair prices".

Loading...

"We want to ease the burden on older Australians and their families and that's exactly why we'll have the Department and Commission conduct investigations and take enforcement action including ordering refunds on behalf of older Australians," Mr Rae said in a statement.

Provider body, Ageing Australia, supported deferring price caps and argued it would have been premature to set caps before an independent cost assessment of the new fee structure was undertaken.

Shadow Aged Care Minister Anne Ruston also said she welcomed the delay because "providers had been given no detail on the design of the price caps and would have had no way of implementing them on the original timeline," but noted the government should have made the decision earlier.

Lengthy delays to monthly statement

Support at Home recipients have also raised concerns about waiting months to receive statements showing how much of their package they have used.

Aged care advocate Hanna Law said she personally had not received her so-called "monthly statement" since December and many others were in the same boat.

It left recipients anxious to avoid overspending and risk being left with a big out-of-pocket bill, but equally not wanting to underspend and miss out on assistance, she said.

If a participant does not fully use their quarterly budget, a maximum of either 10 per cent or $1000 can be rolled over to the next quarter, whichever is higher.

Mr Rae said he was aware of the delays and action was being taken.

"For those providers ignoring their legal obligation to issue monthly statements, the Commission will be monitoring closely and can take regulatory action to protect older Australians," he said.

OPAN said it was told the two main reasons for hold-up were because providers' IT systems were not ready and there was a delay in providers getting the information they needed from Services Australia.

"We certainly would've expected that systems would be in place," Ms Edmonds said, but she understood more people were now finally receiving their statements.

Regardless, Ms Sharkie said the government needed to do "much, much better".

"At every single turn, this system is failing older Australians," she said.

World.title: Meet the staff and volunteers who make Meals on Wheels go round
World.content:
The sweet and sour pork is steaming and ready to be portioned out.

Kitchen supervisor Shay Mitchell has been on the tools since 4:30am getting the food prepared.

He leads a team of staff and volunteers who are well-versed in what to do.

Each staff member has a role at Meals on Wheels in Ipswich to make sure the operation runs smoothly. (ABC News: Jessica van Vonderen)

One scoops up the rice, another the carrots, then the peas and corn.

"Yeah, it works like clockwork," Mr Mitchell said.

"The same things happen in the same order every day."

Brodie Logan volunteers once a week with Meals on Wheels in Ipswich. (ABC News: Jessica van Vonderen)

There's much to do. Ipswich Meals on Wheels is 70 years old, but age has not slowed this operation.

On average, they do 100 hot meals a day, plus desserts, sandwiches and salads.

"I like knowing that the work that I do helps others," Mr Mitchell said.

"That's why I'm still here. It's rewarding work."

Meals on Wheels has been serving in Queensland since 1956. (Supplied: Meals on Wheels)

The early days

Ipswich Meals on Wheels started in 1956, taking inspiration from a similar service in England.

It began in a backyard gardener's cottage, with meals served in a thermos flask and pudding basin for two shillings each.

Meals on Wheels began in Queensland in 1956. (Supplied: Meals on Wheels)

Fast-forward seven decades and the service is now in 140 locations across Queensland, offering low-cost meals to nearly 24,000 customers.

There are about 6,300 volunteers, but they always need more.

'The heart of our business'

Bec Dakin is the general manager of Ipswich Meals on Wheels.

It's in her blood. Four generations of her family have volunteered with the organisation — her grandfather, her mother, and now her two teenage kids, Oscar and Georgia, also pitch in.

Bec Dakin’s mum and grandfather were involved with Meals on Wheels and now her kids Oscar, 18, and Georgia, 16, also volunteer. (ABC News: Jessica Van Vonderen)

"It's helping the community. I feel like she taught me that at a very young age and it's still something I value," Oscar said.

"(Volunteers) are literally the heart of our business," Ms Dakin said.

"We are always indebted to them."

Former railway man Dennis Ellis offers his time and car as one of the regular delivery drivers.

Dennis Ellis is a volunteer driver for Meals on Wheels in Ipswich. (ABC News: Charlie McLean)

It's the friendships that keep him coming back.

"It's being able to really talk to some of the people we deliver meals to," Mr Ellis said.

"You do get very close to some of these people.

"Some ladies say, 'can you go and post this mail for me and while you're doing that would you mind picking up a bottle of milk?'

"I really enjoy it and I'll keep doing it as long as I can."

Meals on Wheels in Ipswich is celebrating its 70th birthday. (ABC News: Charlie McLean)

Care and connection

They do it for people like Sam and Glenda Carroll.

The retired school teachers get a hot lunch delivered most days.

"We've probably been [customers] for about four years now," Mr Carroll said.

"The way we got involved ... is that I broke my jaw and I needed pureed food.

"We get a regular meal at lunch time, so it's very nice."

Bec Dakin is hopeful Meal on Wheels will receive government support to cover the extra fuel costs. (ABC News: Charlie McLean)

Ms Dakin said every meal comes with a welfare check and a conversation.

"It's really about care and connection and we just happen to deliver meals," she said.

Next six months to be 'horrific': Food charities hit by fuel price rises Charities supplying food relief to struggling Australians are grappling with the twin pressures of rising demand for help while their own fuel bills soar.

But like many others, the organisation has been under pressure recently.

"The fuel prices have gone up so much that there are some of our volunteers now that have been seeking some reimbursement, which we do offer them," says Ms Dakin.

"At this point in time, we haven't increased our prices for our clients.

"We are hoping we might get some extra funding from the government shortly to cover the extra costs for fuel.

"That's just wait and see."

World.title: James Murdoch buys New York magazine, Vox podcasts for $419 million
World.content:
Updated BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing James Murdoch buys New York magazine, Vox podcasts for $419 million Christopher Palmeri Updated May 21, 2026 — 5:43am ,first published 1:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

James Murdoch has agreed to buy a significant chunk of Vox Media for more than $US300 million ($419 million), marking a major expansion into US media for the younger son of Australian media mogul Rupert Murdoch. In the deal announced on Wednesday (US time), James Murdoch’s Lupa Systems, a media and technology holding company, will acquire Vox’s podcast network and New York magazine, a publication once owned by Murdoch senior. James Murdoch in 2023. David Paul Morris Other properties owned by Vox Media, including technology website The Verge and lifestyle publication Popsugar, aren’t included in the deal. Financial terms weren’t disclosed, but Murdoch had offered $US300 million for the properties, which include popular shows such as Pivot with Kara Swisher and culture news sites including The Cut and Intelligencer. People familiar with the matter told The New York Times the deal was more than $US300 million.



“This acquisition aligns well with our existing holdings and investments and reflects both our interest in the forward edge of culture and our deep commitment to ambitious journalism and agenda-setting conversations,” Murdoch said in the statement. “It will allow us to apply new tools across the businesses we are building, adding substantial production, distribution, and editorial capability to our group.” The deal marks the first notable transaction since Murdoch cashed out the last of his share of the family’s interest in News Corp and Fox Corp last year as part of a $US3.3 billion ($4.6 billion) agreement with his father and siblings to resolve an acrimonious succession battle. James Murdoch (right) has bought the New York magazine, previously owned by his father Rupert Murdoch (centre). AP Lupa Systems, which Murdoch founded in 2019, has made a number of investments in media as well as businesses tied to pop culture, including a streaming service in India and the parent company of the Art Basel fairs. Earlier this year, Murdoch revealed plans to launch a new ideas expo in Switzerland.



Murdoch, 53, clashed at times with his father and older brother Lachlan over management and editorial direction of the family’s media empire, which includes the Wall Street Journal, Fox News and the New York Post. In 2000, Murdoch left the board of News Corp, citing “disagreements over certain editorial content published by the company’s news outlets and certain other strategic decisions.” He and his wife Kathryn have criticised the way his family’s papers have covered climate issues. Related Article Updated

Media & marketing James Murdoch makes $418m offer for US media assets: report In an interview with The New York Times published on Wednesday, Murdoch said the fact that his father had once owned New York magazine had no special significance. He said he was interested in “thoughtful journalism” and was just trying to “build a great business”. Both the print and podcast portions of the business are profitable, according to a person familiar with the deal. Murdoch sees an opportunity to add more shows to the podcast network, building on what he believes is a growing market for unique voices in that medium, said the person, who asked to not be identified because the plans aren’t public. With New York magazine, Murdoch intends to increase online subscriptions.



The Vox podcast network, home to shows including Criminal and Where Should We Begin? with Esther Perel, has been the fastest growing business within Vox Media and will immediately put Lupa at the top of the podcast field, according to the company. The new Vox Media will be led by co-founder Jim Bankoff, who has led the company since its early days as a network of a dozen grassroots sports blogs. World.title: From ‘Buddy’ to Gawn: The top 10 players of the Pendlebury era
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion From ‘Buddy’ to Gawn: The top 10 players of the Pendlebury era Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age May 21, 2026 — 5:40am

May 21, 2026 — 5:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

When Scott Pendlebury was drafted from Gippsland, 21 years ago, I spoke to an official from a rival club to get his unvarnished thoughts on the draft, and how particular clubs had fared. “Collingwood were terrible,” he said. Among the best players of Scott Pendlebury’s era are Chris Judd, Dustin Martin, Lance Franklin and Patrick Dangerfield. Artwork: Aresna Villanueva, photos: AFL Photos, The Age It was an assessment that proved as off the mark as the calls to sack Mark Thompson as Geelong coach in Pendlebury’s first season. The Magpies, as we know, selected a pair of Gippsland kids named (Dale) Thomas and Pendlebury at picks No.2 and No.5, harvesting the maximum return from a descent down the ladder and the generous rules that awarded a priority pick (No.2) for teams that won five games or less, and incentivised teams to tank.



Pendlebury’s career has reflected his distinctive style of play, in that his impact was not as obvious as, say, “Buddy” Franklin’s or “Dusty” Martin’s. He was a stealthy weapon who shredded the opposition with deft changes of direction and smarts. If he were a tennis player, you would say that he was playing a whole point, not just shots; he could see the whole field. New territory: Pendlebury ahead of his 433rd AFL match. AFL Photos Today, he stands as one of a very small group of footballers in the current competition who, one day in the future, will (surely) be ordained as an official Legend in the Australian Football Hall of Fame. Amid the deluge of tributes, praise and financial benefits, it’s worth considering where Pendlebury’s incomplete innings ranks in the AFL’s pantheon, over the course of his career.



He began in 2006, when West Coast and Sydney were the premier teams, and a young Chris Judd the competition’s best player, soon to be challenged, as Geelong took flight, by Gary Ablett jnr and then the highly unorthodox Franklin. Unlike Dusty, Ablett jnr, Judd, Marcus Bontempelli and Buddy, Pendlebury was never viewed as the No.1 player in the competition, though he was close to Ablett jnr from 2013 and 2014; it is a quirk of his career that peak Pendlebury coincided with a Collingwood recession; four of his five best and fairests were taken from 2013 to 2016. This observer places only four footballers ahead of Pendlebury over the past 20 years. Franklin is foremost, as the era’s generational forward and match-winner – a forward who defied congestion and the flood of defensive numbers to surpass 1000 goals; Buddy did not pack mark, and had periods of spraying shots. But he was an extraordinary and durable champion, who got people out of their seats almost every week. Ablett jnr, aka “Little Gary”, has the game’s best resume in the 21st century, with five most valuable player awards from his peers, a couple of Brownlows, and a machine-like constancy of output (in which he resembles Pendlebury).



Was Ablett superior to the 2020s benchmark individual, “the Bont”? Only by a weensy margin, and Bontempelli – just 30, eight years Pendlebury’s junior – could yet overtake him. Editor's pick AFL 2026 This AFL rule causes outrage and confusion. Two coaches love it Judd’s early years at West Coast were phenomenal. Long-time West Coast chief executive Trevor Nisbett, not prone to hyperbole, once opined that Judd was the best player he had seen. Pendlebury’s career is a contrast to Dusty’s, in the same way that Martin’s is completely different to Kevin Bartlett’s marathon excellence. Martin was a clear best player in the AFL from 2017 to 2019, when he owned the September stage like no player. On the eve of Dusty’s 300th, ex-teammate Shane Edwards explained how those winning Tiger teams gained confidence from knowing that they had Martin; they only needed to get the footy in his vicinity, forward of centre, in a tight game, to win.



Pendlebury’s more muted style was still heavily influential in the clutch moments, none more important than the two grand finals Collingwood won, the 2010 replay (when he was Norm Smith medallist) and the 2023 thriller, when he acted as the on-field director, Luke Hodge-style, in the second half, as the Pies won a classic. Joel Selwood, another destined for Legend-hood, is next behind Dusty at No.7, which is also – unfortunately for Carlton, Essendon and North Melbourne – where he was selected in the 2006 draft. Not as powerful as Buddy, nor as explosive as Judd, Patrick Dangerfield or Martin, Selwood’s aversion to defeat and competitive animus was nonpareil. He was dynamic whenever the Cats needed to arrest the opposition momentum and while combative, his outside game was undersold. Joel Selwood (right, pictured here with Patrick Dangerfield after the 2022 grand final) was as courageous as they come. Eddie Jim Dangerfield, ranked eighth, has claims to being higher on this list, considering his longevity, immense speed and power, and capacity to play forward as well as in the midfield. He was the premier AFL performer in 2016, and not far from in 2015 and 2017-19. The only blemish in his game was that his kicking was much less precise than other champions.



Luke Hodge, who won four flags at Hawthorn and captained three of those sides, could have made the list. AFL Photos The final two spots in the top 10 could be filled by 10 players. I’ve opted for Matthew Pavlich, despite his career beginning way back in 2000, at No.9. Pavlich was far more than an outstanding key forward. He could win games from the midfield, or dominate from behind the ball. Had he played for a monstrous Melbourne team, he’d be even more venerated. “Super Pav” booted 700 goals, and it is a measure of the Swiss army knife superstar that he was picked in five different positions in All-Australian teams (once, erroneously, at full-back). Yes, he played great footy pre-Pendlebury, but his 11 years from 2006 still suffice. At No.10 is another current player, like Pendlebury, who has not gone gently into his mid-30s. Max Gawn, a loose unit in his dissolute youth and slow-burn superstar, is the code’s outstanding ruckman this century, and the best since Simon Madden.



Luke Hodge and Nick Riewoldt would likely make the list if it was a dozen, and some will place them in the top 10 or higher. Nat Fyfe, too, had serious claims given his two Brownlows, but he did not sustain performance into his 30s, when the footy gods struck him down with injury and his output slumped. Jonathan Brown was another brave and battered superstar whose peak ranged from 2003 until 2008 or 2009, not quite enough, even though he was the closest approximation to Wayne Carey in the 2000s. Pendlebury’s capacity to stop time, both when he gains possession, and over the course of his 21 years in the AFL, is his trademark. My top 10 players of the Scott Pendlebury era (since 2006)



Lance Franklin Gary Ablett jnr Marcus Bontempelli Chris Judd Scott Pendlebury Dustin Martin Joel Selwood Patrick Dangerfield Matthew Pavlich Max Gawn Scroll down for profiles of each of the top 10, including some of their most notable (though not all) achievements.
